newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan c.bank won't adjust policy to cool stocks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan c.bank won't adjust policy to cool stocks.

text.p: Central bank chief Hsu Yuan-dong said on Wednesday the bank would not adjust monetary policy to cool Taiwan's red-hot stock market, saying such moves were no "cure all" in the face of concerns of overheating.

"Monetary policy is no cure-all medicine," Hsu told reporters when asked whether the central bank planned to tighten its longstanding "stable to loose, but not too loose" monetary policy to cool what some see as a worrying stock rally.
"The central bank will closely monitor the stock market, but investors should rationally decide when to buy or sell stocks," said the bank governor.

Hsu's bank's repeated issuance of negotiable certificates of deposit in recent weeks has been seen widely as a bid to dampen the sizzling stock market by slowing what have been huge flows of liquidity out of the money market and into the bourse.

Many analysts suggest the stock rally has been fuelled to a large extent by Taiwan's generally loose liquidity situation, which the central bank has tolerated to give a still-sluggish economic recovery the best chance of taking hold.
The central bank has rejected such an explicit link, calling its actions a more general response to fine-tune money supply.
Bank governor Hsu flatly declined to say whether the stock market was overheated.
"It's up to investors to decide whether stocks have been over-valued," Hsu said.

A long bull run in Taiwan's bourse, whose index has notched a series of seven-year highs in recent weeks, has prompted some analysts to begin questioning whether the stock market's economic fundamentals justified such a sustained rise.
The index has soared more than 100 percent since March 1996.
On Wednesday, Taiwan stocks soared to an intraday high 9,648.43, but lost momentum in the final hour and settled for a loss of 11.42 points or 0.12 percent, finishing at 9,544.56.
Hsu said the stock market movements were not the only factor when deciding the monetary policy.
"The stock market is only one part of the financial market. The economy, except for the electronics sector, has not fully recovered yet," he said.
